title: The Trigger, Not the Threshold: What Actually Gets an Owner to Call a Fractional CFO
linkedin:
Ask an owner when they decided to bring in extra financial support, and almost none of them name a revenue figure.

They describe a moment instead.

A bank asked for a forward cash view they couldn't answer with confidence. A decision landed on the desk bigger than any they'd made before. The monthly numbers kept arriving on time, but somehow stopped feeling useful.

We see this pattern constantly across owner-led businesses on the East Coast. Readiness gets framed in terms of size, a million dollars in revenue, a certain headcount. Size is a fine benchmark for a conversation. It is a poor predictor of the actual day someone picks up the phone.

Three moments come up far more often than any revenue figure. A lender wanting a forward view instead of last year's financials. Growth outrunning the reporting rhythm until the bank balance and the ledger quietly drift apart. A decision bigger than the usual ones landing with no one to pressure test it first.

None of these arrive on a schedule. Waiting for a tidier, larger version of the business to show up first usually just means the moment gets managed alone, under pressure, with whatever information happens to be on hand.

The trigger is a far more reliable signal than the threshold ever was.

Full piece on the ProfitPulse blog.

A pattern we see constantly with owner-led businesses across Brisbane, Queensland, and the East Coast: the decision to bring in extra financial support rarely comes down to a revenue figure. It comes down to a specific moment.

Three moments show up more than any others. A bank asks for a forward cash flow view during a facility increase or refinance, and the business realises its reporting has only ever looked backward. Revenue and the team grow, but the monthly numbers keep arriving on the same old lag, and the owner can feel the read slipping between the bank balance and the ledger. Or a decision bigger than the usual ones lands on the desk, an acquisition, a capital raise, a big lease, a senior hire, and there is no one at the table who has made that call before.

None of these arrive on a convenient schedule. Waiting for a tidier, bigger version of the business to show up first usually just means the moment gets handled alone, under pressure, with whatever information is on hand at the time.

If one of these sounds familiar, that is usually a better signal than any number on the P&L. Read the full piece on the ProfitPulse blog for the detail behind each of these three triggers.
